blocks.title: Game Design Document
blocks.subtitle: A complete, production-ready template
blocks.tagline: One document, ten tabs, and the diagrams a game team actually uses. Replace every blue placeholder. Keep the grey instructions until the section is signed off.

blocks.x: READ THIS FIRST
How to use this document
This tab explains the workflow, the typography, the quality bar, and the review gates. Read it once, then work through the numbered tabs in order.
Do not fill the whole document before the prototype. A GDD is a decision tool, not a novel. Write only what the team needs to make the next decision.
1. What this document is

A game design document is the shared source of truth for **what the game is, how it plays, and why those choices are right**. It is not a pitch deck, a technical manual, or a production schedule, although it links to all three. Its job is to keep a multidisciplinary team aligned long enough to ship.

This template is organised as tabs so each discipline can work without scrolling through a hundred pages. The tabs are ordered by the decisions a project makes: vision, gameplay, narrative, experience, art, technology, production, and the diagrams that connect them. Appendices hold the memory of the project: decisions, open questions, references, and sign-off.
Treat the document as **living**. Update it when a decision changes, not at the end of the milestone. A GDD that is six weeks stale is worse than no GDD because people still trust it.
Internal and external versions

Keep one canonical internal copy with the instruction blocks visible. Before sharing with a publisher, platform holder, or external contractor, make a copy, delete every grey instruction and every blue placeholder that is not relevant, and export a PDF. Never maintain two handwritten versions.
2. The ten-step workflow

x: Duplicate this document (File → Make a copy). Keep one canonical copy and link it from the project hub. Do not fork it per discipline.
Fill **01 Vision & Strategy** first. Get sign-off on the one-page pitch before writing a single system.
Fill **02 Gameplay & Systems** only to the depth the current prototype can test. Mark everything else as an open question.
Use **08 Diagram Playbook** to draw the five diagrams that pay for themselves: game flow, core loop, systems map, one state machine, one level flow.
Fill **03 Narrative & World** to the scope the game can actually carry. Do not write a novel the budget cannot produce.
Fill **04 Experience: UX, UI, Audio** with the screen flow and accessibility commitments before UI production starts.
Fill **05 Art & Content** and **06 Technical Design** in parallel with the vertical slice. Each claim must be validated by a real asset or a real build.
Fill **07 Production & Launch** last, using real velocity from the prototype rather than optimism.
Review at every gate. Record decisions and rejected alternatives in **09 Appendices**, not in chat threads.
Freeze scope at alpha. After that, every change goes through the change log and a named approver.

blocks.x: 3. Typography legend
Four type styles carry four different jobs. The style tells you whether you are reading structure, content, guidance, or an example.

items.label: Montserrat · Headings
items.desc: Tab names, section titles, table headers. Never use it for body copy.

items.label: Lato · Your content
items.sample: The player crosses the ridge before the storm reaches the valley.
items.desc: Everything you write about the game. This is the voice of the document.

items.label: Roboto Mono · Instructions
items.sample: // Write the loop as three verbs. Name the feedback for each.
items.desc: Grey guidance for the author. Delete before external publication.

items.label: Playfair Display · Examples
items.sample: “A good loop is legible in one breath.”
items.desc: Quotes, reference copy, and worked examples. Never a requirement.

items.label: Lato italic · Placeholders
items.desc: Blue italic text is a question to your team. Every one must be answered or deleted.

blocks.x: 4. GDD versus the other documents
Teams get into trouble when one document tries to do every job. Keep these artefacts separate and link them.

head: Document
Question it answers
Owner
When
rows: Should we make this at all?
What are we making, and how does it play?
How is it built, and how do we keep it running?
When, by whom, and with what budget?
Why should you fund or publish this?
What does it look like, exactly?
What is true about the world and its people?

blocks.x: 5. The quality bar
A section is ready for review when a new team member could implement or critique it without asking you what you meant. Use these six tests.

x: **Every mechanic has a verb, an input, an immediate feedback, and a failure state.** If one is missing, the mechanic is not specified.
**Every number has a unit, a range, and an owner.** “Fast” is not a value; “0.35 s recovery, tuned by combat design” is.
**Every feature has an owner and a milestone.** Unowned work is not planned work.
**Every claim about the player is backed by a playtest, a reference, or an explicit assumption.** Label assumptions so they can be tested.
**Every diagram answers one question and carries a legend.** A diagram that needs a paragraph of explanation is a table in disguise.
**No “fun”, “engaging”, or “immersive” without a measurable definition.** Say what the player does, sees, and feels, and how you will know.

blocks.label: THE TEST
blocks.x: If you cannot describe how you would test it, it is not a design decision yet. It is a hope.
6. Review gates
Each gate is a decision, not a status meeting. If the exit criteria are not met, the project does not advance; it cuts scope or returns to the previous gate.

head: Gate
What must be true
Who signs off
rows: Pillars, audience, core loop, and scope are credible for the team and budget.
The core loop is playable; the fun hypothesis has been tested with real players.
One polished 15-minute slice proves the pipelines, art direction, audio, and performance.
All features are in; the game can be played start to finish, even with placeholder content.
Content is locked; only bugs, balance, and polish remain.
Certification passed; store, support, and live operations are ready.
KPIs reviewed; patch cadence and content roadmap are operating.

blocks.x: 8. Owners and decision rights
One person is accountable for each decision. Everyone else is consulted or informed. This table prevents the most common failure mode in game development: a decision with three owners and no owner.
9. Change log

Log every material change: a pillar, a mechanic, a scope cut, a platform, a date. Trivial wording edits do not need an entry. The log is how a new team member understands why the game looks the way it does.

blocks.x: 10. Sign-off

Sign-off means the signatory has read the section, agrees with the decisions, and accepts the scope implied by them. It does not mean the section will never change; it means changes now require a logged decision.
